name: Schistosoma japonicum

taxonomy.rank_note: Reference groups can include multiple species. Protozoan higher-rank systems differ; the lineage is provided without forcing every clade into a class rank.

morphology: Egg: approximately 70–100 × 55–64 µm, with wider ranges in comparative references; rounded to oval, nonoperculated with an inconspicuous lateral spine or knob and a miracidium.
Adults occupy mesenteric veins; eggs traverse intestinal tissue.

transmission.detail: Waterborne cercariae from infected snails penetrate skin; adult pairs develop in venous vessels and release eggs that can reach feces.

life_cycle.detail: Waterborne cercariae from infected snails penetrate skin; adult pairs develop in venous vessels and release eggs that can reach feces.
Embryonated eggs in stool; tissue eggs may also be demonstrated.

hosts: Definitive: humans; animal reservoirs vary by species. Intermediate: freshwater snail.
distribution: Focal transmission in China, the Philippines and Indonesia; travel-related differential in Thailand.
clinical_significance: Intestinal inflammation and chronic hepatosplenic disease; retained eggs drive granulomatous pathology.
specimen: Embryonated eggs in stool; tissue eggs may also be demonstrated.
diagnostics: Stool concentration or quantitative egg microscopy at 100–400×; low-intensity infection may need additional validated tests.
differential_diagnosis: S. mekongi and S. japonicum eggs overlap; lateral projections may be hidden by orientation. Geography supports but does not prove identification.
review_status: Source-compiled educational content; not independently clinically validated
description: Schistosoma japonicum — Asian intestinal blood fluke. Intestinal inflammation and chronic hepatosplenic disease; retained eggs drive granulomatous pathology.

annotation_guidance: Record specimen, stage, stain, objective/total magnification, pixel calibration, source image and reviewer certainty.
Native crops of 200–650 pixels do not determine biological size. Retain µm-per-pixel calibration before resizing.
Split training, validation and test data by patient/specimen; keep related crops in the same split.
Keep damaged or ambiguous objects uncertain. Molecular confirmation of a mixed specimen does not assign every pictured object a species.
